name: Yara Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the primary crusher and the conveyors at a large open-pit lithium mine. The trucks tip ore into the crusher, it breaks the rock down, and my job is keeping it all flowing from the control panel and out on the walkways, watching for blockages, belt wander, bearings running hot. Twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off. I love the puzzle of it, when the whole system hums at full rate you feel like a conductor. What wears me out is the night shifts and the alarms, there's always an alarm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the control panel. How do you use technology in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly, I'm the one in the crew who's always fiddling. I use an AI assistant every day to write my handover notes and to look at the vibration data from the conveyor bearings, it spots patterns before I would. Last year I did a drone pilot licence on my own time, just because. Dev, my partner, teaches maths at the high school, our girls are grown, Mia's a vet and Zoe's a plumber. We've got savings, shares and a rental house, so I'm in a lucky spot and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd probably post that on the mining forum I read, with some numbers about what it actually saved us. No drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AI Plateau means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing, just with a slightly better assistant. Honestly, I'd be a touch disappointed, I enjoy new toys. But my retirement plans don't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep using the tools for handovers and bearing data. I'd probably start doing some drone survey work on my days off for local farmers, checking fences and dams. Small money, but fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bored. Like a holiday where the weather's just fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI daily. What would AI Plateau mean for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It saves me maybe forty minutes a shift on notes and catches one or two bearing problems a month. That's real, but it's not world-changing. I'd keep using it the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with that drone licence, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fly it for farmers on my off days. Maybe I'd turn it into a little side business once I retire, aerial photos, stockpile measurements. I like having a project.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool, not a miracle, and I'd post on the mining forum with numbers on what it actually saved us. No drama.
S0.think: She thinks she keeps doing her job with a slightly better assistant, and her retirement plans don't change. She'd be a touch disappointed because she enjoys new tools.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI for handovers and bearing data. Starts small drone survey jobs for local farmers on her days off, checking fences and dams.
S0.feel: Calm and a little bored, like a holiday where the weather's just fine.
S0.quote: Like a holiday where the weather's just fine.
S0.fieldNote: Yara is a tinkerer who measures what AI saves her, about forty minutes a shift. She already has a drone licence earned on her own time. Her money is secure with savings, shares and a rental house, and she knows she's lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on the front foot, learn the systems now. I'd tell the crew the people who know the software will be the last ones they let go. I'd say it without preaching, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think Steady Disruption means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's probably good. The crusher's already half automated, the next step is a remote operations room running three crushers at once, and I'd want that job. I'd be one of the people running the machines, not one of the people replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the remote control room the day it's advertised. I'd keep learning, maybe a short course in process control at the technical college. And I'd grow the drone work on weekends, stockpile surveys for smaller quarries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, interested. Like the start of a new season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle most with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kenny on B crew, he's fifty-five and hates the computer, he still prints his roster. He's a brilliant fitter with his hands. I'd worry for him and I'd sit with him and show him the basics if he'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're in a lucky spot. Does that change how you'd talk about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I try not to tell people it's easy when it's easy for me. I've got a rental house and a partner on a steady wage, Kenny's got a mortgage and a wife who's sick. That's not the same starting line.

S1.say: I'd tell the crew to get on the front foot and learn the systems now, because the people who know the software will be the last let go. I'd try to say it without preaching.
S1.think: She thinks it's probably good for her, since a remote room running three crushers would be a job she wants. She sees herself running the machines, not being replaced by them.
S1.do: Applies for the remote control room the day it's advertised and takes a short process-control course at the technical college. Grows her weekend drone work into stockpile surveys for smaller quarries.
S1.feel: Calm and interested, like the start of a new season.
S1.quote: Kenny's got a mortgage and a wife who's sick. That's not the same starting line.
S1.fieldNote: She is aware her security makes change easier for her than for colleagues like Kenny. Her plan is to move up into control and build a side business. She offers personal help rather than political answers, in keeping with her pragmatic centre views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be messy, and the government and companies need to agree on a plan fast. I wouldn't pretend I have the answer. I'd share whatever useful information I found, that's what I'm good for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2028 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even the control room goes, because if the AI can do any job, it can watch a crusher. So I'm out at sixty, comfortably, but out. The drone side business probably goes too, the drones will fly themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd move some of the shares into the companies making the robots, if I can't beat them I'd like a slice. I'd take a package at sixty if offered. Then I'd look for whatever new work appears around the machines, setting them up, checking them, because there's always something at the edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my bills, more like a game I was good at just got rewritten without asking me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty when this lands. Does even the remote room survive full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, probably not. There'll be a stage where the robots need people to supervise them, but with full AGI that stage might be short. I'd still try, I'd rather be in the room than outside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would two years change the drone idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It turns into a hobby. I'd buy a better drone and fly it over the lake for fun. Two years isn't long enough to build a business that the machines can't swallow.

S2.say: I'd say it's going to be messy and government and companies need to agree on a plan fast. I wouldn't pretend to have the answer, but I'd share any useful information I found.
S2.think: She believes even the control room goes, because an AI that can do any job can watch a crusher, so she's out at sixty, comfortably. Her drone side business likely goes too, since drones will fly themselves.
S2.do: Moves some shares into robot-making companies in the first month and takes a package at sixty if offered. Looks for new work at the edges of the machines, such as setting them up and checking them.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not about bills but because a game she was good at got rewritten without asking her.
S2.quote: A game I was good at just got rewritten without asking me.
S2.fieldNote: Two years removes the ladder her adaptability usually gives her. She stays practical, hedging by investing in robot makers and looking for edge work. Her drone side business shrinks to a hobby in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a decent plan if people actually use it. Don't wait for someone else to fix it. Learn something, save something, talk to your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2031 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a few good years in the remote room, then go around sixty-two or sixty-three on my own terms. That's close to what I'd planned anyway. So for me it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, into the control room and the process course. I'd build up the drone survey work into something real, with a proper business name, while there's still demand. And I'd shift some money into the robot side of the market slowly, not all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what does five give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can be ahead of the curve instead of under it. In two, I'm just watching. In five, I've got time to set up something useful before it gets swallowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd tell Zoe, being a plumber?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zoe's tough, she'd figure it out. I'd tell her the robots will need plumbers to install them before they replace plumbers. And I'd tell her to put money away now, because her hands are her pension.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a decent plan if people use it, and not to wait for someone else to fix it. Learn something, save something and talk to your family.
S3.think: She expects a few good years in the remote room and leaving around sixty-two or sixty-three on her own terms. That's close to her plan, so it's fine for her.
S3.do: Moves into the control room and takes the process course in year one. Builds the drone survey work into a proper business while demand lasts, and gradually shifts some money into robot-related shares.
S3.quote: Five years means I can be ahead of the curve instead of under it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for her adaptability to work in her favour again. She plans the business with a clear sense it may be swallowed eventually. Her advice to her plumber daughter blends practicality with care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd probably write something on the forum about how to plan for it, step by step. People like a checklist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2036 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be retired by then, probably running the drone business part-time until the robots take that too. It doesn't threaten me. It actually sounds interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, move into the control room when it comes, learn everything. Build the drone business slowly over the decade. Retire around sixty-three and keep the business as a hobby that pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, curious. I'd quite like to see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: By 2036 you'd be sixty-eight. What does this one look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it's fun. If they need someone to teach people to work alongside the robots, I'd do that till seventy. I hate the idea of sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep working past your planned retirement, if it were interesting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the girls to stay curious. That's the only real advice I've got, the rest is luck.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift so use it, and I'd write a step-by-step planning checklist on the forum because people like a checklist.
S4.think: She expects to be retired by then and running her drone business part-time until robots take that too. It doesn't threaten her and actually sounds interesting.
S4.do: Keeps working and moves into the control room when it comes, learning everything she can. Builds the drone business slowly over the decade and retires around sixty-three, keeping the business as a paying hobby.
S4.feel: Calm and curious about what happens.
S4.quote: I'd do that till seventy. I hate the idea of sitting still.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she frames AGI as interesting rather than threatening. She'd happily work past retirement if the work were fun. Her advice to her daughters comes down to staying curious, and she credits the rest to luck.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mostly for people like Kenny, not for me. What would help is good, honest information early, and training that starts before the jobs go, not after, with some help for people who aren't confident with computers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how many miners already use AI. More than you'd think. We're not all dinosaurs, some of us run the night shift on it.

headlineQuote: I'd be one of the people running the machines, not one of the people replaced by them.
portrait: Yara Abbott is a 58-year-old crusher and conveyor operator at a large open-pit lithium mine who uses AI every day and earned a drone licence on her own time. With savings, shares and a rental house, she knows she is luckier than colleagues like Kenny, who has a mortgage and a sick wife. In the slower pictures she plans to move into the remote control room and grow a drone survey business. The two-year AGI picture leaves her financially fine but uneasy that the game she was good at gets rewritten. With five or ten years she is calm and curious, planning to stay ahead of the curve.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, mainly for less confident colleagues like Kenny rather than for herself.
whatWouldHelp: Good, honest information early and training that starts before jobs go, with help for people who aren't confident with computers.
